provenance: Growth-faltering thresholds follow the WHO child growth standards and the widely used 0.67 z-score criterion for a clinically significant downward centile crossing; acute-malnutrition cut-offs follow WHO/UNICEF community-based management of severe acute malnutrition. This engine interprets z-scores that were computed and stamped at the time of measurement by pct-service — it never recomputes them, so a stored score and its interpretation cannot drift apart. Thresholds and actions are an engineering seed and are NOT a ratified national protocol. See docs/clinical-governance/edliz-engineering-seed-policy.md.

signals.name: Implausible change between measurements
signals.action: Do not act on this trend. A change this large between contacts is far more often a measurement or transcription error than real growth — check the scale, the recorded date and whether these two measurements belong to the same child.

signals.name: Trend not derived across a change of growth standard
signals.action: Do not read a rise or fall between these two contacts. They were scored against different growth references — an infant born preterm is read on the Fenton 2013 preterm chart until it ends at 50 weeks postmenstrual, and on the WHO standard at corrected age after that — so the step between them belongs to the charts, not to the child. Judge this contact on its own weight, classification and clinical picture, and read the trend from the next measurement on the same reference.

signals.name: Apparent drop explained by the switch from length to height
signals.action: Do not act on this apparent loss. Standing height measures about 0.7 cm less than recumbent length in the same child, and the standards change at two years to match. Confirm on the next visit before treating this as faltering.

signals.name: Severe growth faltering
signals.action: Assess for underlying illness including tuberculosis and HIV, assess feeding directly rather than by report, and refer for nutritional management. A drop of two thresholds is rarely explained by feeding technique alone.

signals.name: Absolute weight loss
signals.action: A child who has lost weight since the last contact needs assessment today: look for illness, feeding difficulty and food insecurity in the household. Do not wait for the next scheduled visit.

signals.name: Growth faltering
signals.action: Assess feeding by observing a feed, check for illness, counsel the carer, and weigh again in two weeks rather than at the next routine visit. Faltering is visible in the trend long before any single measurement crosses a classification line.

signals.name: No weight gain
signals.action: A child under two who has not gained weight in two months is faltering even if their weight-for-age has not yet crossed a threshold. Assess feeding and illness now.

signals.name: Head circumference crossing centiles
signals.action: Head growth crossing centiles in either direction needs neurological assessment: accelerating growth can mean raised intracranial pressure, and decelerating growth can be the first sign of a developmental problem. Confirm the measurement before referring.

signals.name: Catch-up growth
signals.action: Weight-for-age is rising. Continue the current feeding plan and keep the child under review until the gain is sustained across two contacts — a single good weight can be a wet nappy.

testCases.name: a z drop of 0.9 is faltering
a z drop of 1.5 is severe and needs referral
an implausible jump blocks interpretation rather than reporting faltering
the length-to-height switch is not treated as faltering
recovering weight is reported as catch-up
the step at the Fenton-to-WHO handover is not reported as faltering
a large step across the handover is refused rather than blocking interpretation
weight genuinely lost across the handover is still reported
two contacts on the preterm chart are compared normally
a single measurement cannot show a trend
